summary: Defines a SASL mechanism for one-time passwords, so applications can use OTP authentication in a formal, standard way instead of ad-hoc parsing. It updates RFC 2222. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A one-time password is like a ticket that works only once. This lets many programs ask for such a ticket in the same standard way.

questions: what is the otp sasl mechanism
how do one-time passwords work with sasl
what is an otp extended response
subtitle: How to plug one-time passwords into any SASL-enabled protocol in one standard way.

tldr.problem: One-time passwords (OTP) were being added to application protocols in an ad-hoc fashion with heuristic parsing, so clients and servers could not count on compatible behavior.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2444 defines a single SASL mechanism named OTP. The client sends an authorization identity and an authentication identity, the server replies with an OTP challenge, and the client answers with an extended response in hex or six-word form.
tldr.outcome: It replaces the SKEY SASL mechanism, which it marks OBSOLETE, and updates RFC 2222. It gives no session privacy, no server authentication and no protection from active attacks.

today: RFC 2444 is a Proposed Standard from October 1998. It updates RFC 2222, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why OTP Needs a SASL Mechanism
sections.content:
The one-time password system (RFC 2289) is useful where there is limited client or server trust. Until this RFC, OTP was added to protocols in an ad-hoc fashion with heuristic parsing. RFC 2444 defines an OTP mechanism for SASL (RFC 2222), so OTP can be integrated formally into many application protocols.

The text assumes the reader already knows OTP, OTP extended responses (RFC 2243) and SASL. It names IMAP, ACAP, POP3 and LDAPv3 as protocols that can use it.
sections.plainLanguage: Before this, every program asked for one-time passwords in its own made-up way. This RFC gives them all the same words to use.

sections.title: Intended Use
sections.content:
The OTP mechanism replaces the SKEY SASL mechanism. It suits cases where the client is untrusted, such as a kiosk, because a one-time password gives the client only a single opportunity to act for the user.

It is also a good fit where interactive logins to the server are permitted. A compromised OTP authentication database is only subject to dictionary attacks, unlike the databases of simple mechanisms such as CRAM-MD5 (RFC 2195).

One thing to remember: each use of the mechanism causes the user's entry in the authentication database to be updated.
sections.plainLanguage: If you use a shared computer you do not trust, a ticket that works once is safe. Even if the computer copies it, the copy is already used up.

sections.title: Profiling OTP for SASL
sections.content:
OTP and its extended responses have many options, and authentication only works if client and server have compatible sets. This RFC picks one profile for the single mechanism named OTP.

  • The extended response syntax MUST be used.
  • Servers MUST support the extended responses hex, word, init-hex and init-word. They MUST support word and init-word for the standard dictionary and SHOULD support alternate dictionaries. They MUST NOT require any additional OTP extensions or options.
  • Clients SHOULD be able to show the OTP challenge to the user and accept an OTP in multi-word format. They MAY also accept the pass phrase directly and compute the hex or word response.
  • Clients MUST indicate when authentication fails because the sequence number got too low, and SHOULD offer to reset the sequence with init-hex or init-word.

Support for the MD5 algorithm is REQUIRED and support for SHA1 is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: OTP has lots of optional extras, so this RFC picks one fixed set that everybody must understand. That way a client and a server always have something in common.

sections.title: The Authentication Exchange
sections.content:
The mechanism provides no security layer. The client starts by sending two pieces of information.

  • An authorization identity. The empty string defaults to the authentication identity. It lets administrators or proxy servers log in as a different user. It may be up to 255 octets and ends with a NUL (0) octet.
  • An authentication identity, the identity whose pass phrase is used. It may be up to 255 octets.

US-ASCII printable characters are preferred for both. UTF-8 printable characters are permitted for international names, and other character sets are forbidden.

The server replies with the OTP challenge as defined in RFC 2289 and RFC 2243. On success the client builds an extended response in hex, word, init-hex or init-word form, without unnecessary whitespace and without a required trailing space or newline. Servers MUST tolerate input of any length but MAY fail authentication if it is unreasonably long.

If a client sees an unknown hash algorithm name it cannot process a typed pass phrase. It MAY then ask for the six-word format, cancel and try another SASL mechanism, or close the connection. For this reason a server is restricted to one OTP hash algorithm per user.
sections.plainLanguage: You first say who you are, then the server sends a puzzle, and you send back the answer that only works once.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows the mechanism in the ACAP and IMAP profiles of SASL, for the user tim with no authorization identity. In the ACAP example the server challenge is otp-md5 499 ke1234 ext and the client answers with hex:5bf075d9959d036f for the pass phrase This is a test. The same challenge can be answered in six-word form as word:BOND FOGY DRAB NE RISE MART.

With an otp-sha1 challenge the hex answer is hex:c90fc02cc488df5e. A fourth example uses init-hex to reset the sequence in the same exchange, and the server then says the OTP sequence was reset.

In the IMAP profile there is no initial client response and the data is base64 encoded. The server challenge there is otp-md5 123 ke1234 ext and the client response is hex:11d4c147e227c1f1.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC shows a few pretend logins so you can see what the client says and what the server says back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 2444 adds no security considerations beyond those of SASL, OTP and OTP extended responses, and it summarizes them.

  • The mechanism does not provide session privacy, server authentication or protection from active attacks.
  • It is subject to passive dictionary attacks. Choosing pass phrases well reduces how severe this is.
  • The server's authentication database need not be plaintext-equivalent.
  • Server implementations MUST protect against the race attack described in RFC 2289.
sections.plainLanguage: The ticket only works once, but a stranger can still watch the conversation. Pick a pass phrase that is hard to guess.

sections.title: Names, Languages and IANA
sections.content:
Users are encouraged to restrict user names and pass phrases to US-ASCII. Any characters outside it are interpreted as UTF-8. Server support for alternate dictionaries is strongly RECOMMENDED so the six-word format can use non-English words.

The registration template names the SASL mechanism OTP with intended usage COMMON. The memo also amends the SKEY SASL mechanism registration by changing its intended usage to OBSOLETE.
sections.plainLanguage: The new method gets its official name, OTP, and the old method, SKEY, gets marked as retired.
